newsitem.title: USA: Group calls for changes at Ill. tollway agency.
newsitem.headline: Group calls for changes at Ill. tollway agency.

text.p: A government watchdog group called Monday for fundamental changes in the operation of the Illinois State Toll Highway Authority.
The Elmhurst, Ill.-based Citizen Advocacy Center released a report that claimed the tollway agency has gained "unlimited and unchecked powers at the expense of Illinois motorists."
"The toll authority is an agency run amok and ripe for reform," said Theresa Amato, the center's executive director, in a news release.

The report said that the tollway was perpetuating its existence by failing to remove tolls from already built and financed toll roads, bucking the original intent of state legislation to turn the roads into freeways once they were paid off.

"When the construction of tollways was approved in 1953, toll payers were promised that once they tossed in enough money to pay off the construction bonds of the three original tollways, the tollways would become freeways," the center said. "By 1984, those tollways generated enough money to pay off the construction bonds, but motorists continue to pay tolls to use these roads."

The group recommended several changes including lowering or removing tolls, requiring outside monitoring of the agency, prohibiting the diversion of revenues from existing toll roads to pay for construction of new roads, and requiring competitive bidding for professional contracts.
Dave Loveday, a spokesman for the tollway agency, said some of the group's recommendations have already been undertaken by the authority.
He added, however, that decreasing or removing tolls would impair the authority's approximately $1 billion of debt outstanding.
"We are a system. There can be no (freeways) while we have outstanding debt," he said.
The group's report came on the heels of a U.S. District Court ruling earlier this month that stalled a planned expansion of the tollway system in northeastern Illinois.
Judge Suzanne Conlon ruled that the state had failed to evaluate alternatives to a 12.5-mile, $700 million extension of I-355 and the impact the extension would have on air quality.
Loveday said a decision was expected soon by the tollway board on how it would proceed in the lawsuit brought by several environmental groups.
